variants.title: Run the parsing pipeline
variants.context: Dedoc separates format handling from structure construction: a converter normalizes formats that need it, a reader produces lines, annotations, tables, attachments, and metadata, a structure extractor assigns line types and hierarchy levels, and a constructor builds and serializes the requested representation.
variants.prompt: A legacy office document is submitted and the consumer wants a structured tree. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Extract structure by assigning line types and hierarchy levels.
Read the document into lines, annotations, tables, attachments, and metadata.
Convert the legacy format into the supported container representation.
Construct the requested tree output, serialize it, and retain source lineage.

variants.hint: Which stage is skipped entirely when the format is already supported?
variants.explanation: Conversion, reading, structure extraction, and output construction are separate stages because each failure has a different owner and a different retry.

variants.title: Run the parsing pipeline
variants.context: Dedoc separates format handling from structure construction: a converter normalizes formats that need it, a reader produces lines, annotations, tables, attachments, and metadata, a structure extractor assigns line types and hierarchy levels, and a constructor builds and serializes the requested representation.
variants.prompt: A mixed PDF binder holds native-text pages and scanned inserts. Put the reading work in order.

items.text: Reuse the native text on pages that have a trustworthy layer and recognize only the scanned inserts.
Skip conversion, since the PDF is already a supported representation.
Construct the output and record which route each page took.
Detect the textual layer at page level rather than judging the binder by its first pages.
Assign line types and hierarchy levels across the combined line set.

variants.hint: The first pages of a binder are not evidence about the rest of it.
variants.explanation: Page-level detection is what keeps a mixed binder from paying OCR cost everywhere or losing the scanned inserts entirely.

variants.title: Run the parsing pipeline
variants.context: Dedoc separates format handling from structure construction: a converter normalizes formats that need it, a reader produces lines, annotations, tables, attachments, and metadata, a structure extractor assigns line types and hierarchy levels, and a constructor builds and serializes the requested representation.
variants.prompt: A parsed contract comes back with lines and headings but no table objects, and the consumer requires tables. Put the response in order.

items.text: Reparse with table analysis enabled or route the document to the fallback parser.
Publish the versioned output only once it satisfies the consumer contract.
Classify the result as a contract failure because required objects are missing.
Move the job to review required instead of publishing partial structure.
Validate the output against the required parsed-output shape rather than trusting the successful response.

variants.hint: A successful response is not the same as a usable result.
variants.explanation: The publish gate checks the fields the consumer needs, so an incomplete parse becomes a review task rather than silently degraded downstream data.

variants.title: Move a job through the service
variants.context: The parser supplies parsing; the surrounding service supplies admission control, routing, isolation, and a publish gate. Jobs move through accepted, queued, running, and then review required, succeeded, or failed, and retries create new attempts under the same job identity.
variants.prompt: A tenant uploads a document that parses cleanly. Put the production stages in order.

items.text: Validate and publish: check coverage and schema, store immutable input and output references, and publish a versioned result.
Parse in isolation: run converters, readers, OCR, and table analysis under CPU, memory, and time limits.
Quarantine the input: verify media type, size, page and attachment limits, tenant identity, and an idempotency key.
Route and enqueue: inspect the document profile, select parameters, assign a deadline and retry budget.

variants.hint: Untrusted bytes are contained before any parameter is chosen.
variants.explanation: Admission, routing, parsing, and the publish gate are separate operational stages so a bad input never reaches a worker and a bad output never reaches a consumer.

variants.title: Move a job through the service
variants.context: The parser supplies parsing; the surrounding service supplies admission control, routing, isolation, and a publish gate. Jobs move through accepted, queued, running, and then review required, succeeded, or failed, and retries create new attempts under the same job identity.
variants.prompt: A worker finishes a document after its queue lease has already expired. Put the handling in order.

items.text: A retry started a new attempt under the same job identity.
The job was accepted with an immutable source reference and an idempotency key.
Exactly one versioned output is published for the job.
The late attempt tries to publish and the idempotent publish path rejects the duplicate.
The attempt ran under a worker lease that expired before the parse finished.

variants.hint: The job identity outlives any single attempt.
variants.explanation: Retries create new attempts under one job identity and publishing is idempotent, which is what prevents a lost lease from producing two published results.

variants.title: Move a job through the service
variants.context: The parser supplies parsing; the surrounding service supplies admission control, routing, isolation, and a publish gate. Jobs move through accepted, queued, running, and then review required, succeeded, or failed, and retries create new attempts under the same job identity.
variants.prompt: A 600-page scanned document exceeds its worker memory envelope. Put the states in order, ending with the recorded outcome.

items.text: A worker lease takes the attempt and the parse begins running.
The job is recorded as failed with the reason classified as a resource failure.
A route, a deadline, and a retry budget are recorded and the job is queued.
The attempt is killed for exceeding its per-process memory limit and the retry budget is exhausted.
The input passes admission checks and the job is accepted.

variants.hint: The last state has to say more than that the job did not finish.
variants.explanation: A final reason classified as input, conversion, reader, resource, or contract failure is what routes the fix to the right owner.

variants.title: Size the fleet from page work
variants.context: Fleet sizing runs on page work, not file count. Documents in the window, pages per document, the OCR share, the table-analysis share, and the per-worker memory envelope are independent demand drivers, and averages hide the OCR-heavy tail that sets queue age.
variants.prompt: A tenant sends 900 documents per hour averaging 6 pages each, and 25 percent of pages need OCR. How many OCR pages arrive per hour?
variants.hint: Convert documents into pages before applying any share.
variants.explanation: Demand is page work, so the OCR share applies to incoming pages rather than to documents, which is what exposes the expensive tail.

mistakes.feedback: The 25 percent share was applied to documents instead of to pages.
That is total incoming pages per hour with the OCR share never applied.

variants.title: Size the fleet from page work
variants.context: Fleet sizing runs on page work, not file count. Documents in the window, pages per document, the OCR share, the table-analysis share, and the per-worker memory envelope are independent demand drivers, and averages hide the OCR-heavy tail that sets queue age.
variants.prompt: A native page costs 0.2 seconds of service time and an OCR page costs 1.8 seconds. A 10-page document has 3 scanned pages and 7 native pages. What is its total service time in seconds?
variants.hint: The two page types are priced separately, so bill each group at its own rate.
variants.explanation: Two documents of equal size can have very different service times, which is why capacity is planned from page mix rather than file count.

mistakes.feedback: Every page was charged the OCR rate; only the 3 scanned pages need recognition.
Every page was charged the native rate, which ignores the recognition cost entirely.

variants.title: Size the fleet from page work
variants.context: Fleet sizing runs on page work, not file count. Documents in the window, pages per document, the OCR share, the table-analysis share, and the per-worker memory envelope are independent demand drivers, and averages hide the OCR-heavy tail that sets queue age.
variants.prompt: A host has 32 GB of memory, 5 GB is reserved for the operating system and agents, and each parser worker needs a 1.8 GB envelope. How many concurrent workers fit?
variants.hint: The workers only get what is left after the reservation.
variants.explanation: Per-process memory is an independent demand driver, so concurrency is bounded by the memory envelope rather than by CPU alone.

mistakes.feedback: The 5 GB reservation was spent on workers, which leaves the host with no headroom.
That is the gigabytes available to workers, not the number of workers that fit in them.

variants.title: Classify the final failure
variants.context: A final failure reason is classified as input, conversion, reader, resource, or contract, because each class has a different owner and a different retry. A response that returns successfully but misses required objects is a contract failure, not a success.
variants.prompt: A service records a final reason for every failed job. Match each class to what it means.

pairs.label: Input failure
pairs.detail: The submitted bytes violated media type, size, page, attachment, or malware policy at admission.

pairs.label: Conversion failure
pairs.detail: A format could not be normalized into a supported container representation.

pairs.label: Reader failure
pairs.detail: A supported representation produced no usable lines, tables, attachments, or metadata.

pairs.label: Resource failure
pairs.detail: The attempt exceeded its CPU, memory, or execution-time limit inside the isolated worker.

pairs.label: Contract failure
pairs.detail: Output exists but misses the coverage, objects, or schema version the consumer requires.

variants.hint: Two of these happen before parsing begins and one happens after it finishes.
variants.explanation: Each class has a different owner and a different retry, so collapsing them into one error rate makes the fleet's real problem invisible.

variants.title: Classify the final failure
variants.context: A final failure reason is classified as input, conversion, reader, resource, or contract, because each class has a different owner and a different retry. A response that returns successfully but misses required objects is a contract failure, not a success.
variants.prompt: Five jobs fail in one hour. Match each to the class its final reason should record.

pairs.label: An archive with 40 levels of nested attachments is stopped at admission
A legacy office file cannot be normalized into its newer container format
A supported PDF returns no lines, tables, or metadata at all
A worker is killed for passing its memory envelope on a 600-page scan
A response returns successfully but the required table objects are absent

variants.hint: One of these returned a successful response and still failed.
variants.explanation: A successful response that misses required objects is a contract failure, which is why the publish gate validates the shape the consumer actually needs.

variants.title: Classify the final failure
variants.context: A final failure reason is classified as input, conversion, reader, resource, or contract, because each class has a different owner and a different retry. A response that returns successfully but misses required objects is a contract failure, not a success.
variants.prompt: A second hour brings five more failures. Match each to its class.

pairs.label: An upload whose declared media type is not on the allowed list
A page-level parse that ran past its execution-time limit twice
A supported container whose reader returns lines but crashes on its tables
A published candidate whose schema version the downstream consumer cannot read
A spreadsheet that no converter can turn into a supported representation

variants.hint: Ask which stage was the last one that could still have succeeded.
variants.explanation: Classifying by the stage that actually failed is what makes retries, ownership, and release comparisons meaningful across a document population.

variants.title: Route from the real representation
variants.context: The parser route must match the document's actual representation and the downstream output contract. Reusing a trustworthy native text layer is cheaper and more accurate than recognition, and forcing the image path adds latency and recognition error wherever a usable text layer already exists.
variants.prompt: A batch of legacy office files arrives, and a team proposes rendering every page to an image and running OCR so all formats take one path. What should the reviewer say?
options: Adopt it, since a single uniform path is simpler to operate and to benchmark.
Reject it, and convert the files so the native office reader can read them.
Adopt it only for files whose native reader has failed at least once before.
optionFeedback: Uniformity is bought here by discarding paragraphs, tables, annotations, metadata, and attachments the file already carries.
Native office readers preserve that structure without rendering, so conversion plus the native reader is the cheaper and more accurate route.
A per-file failure history is not a representation check and still sends recoverable documents through recognition.
variants.hint: Ask what the file already contains before deciding what to recover.
variants.explanation: Recognition is for pixels that hold no usable text, so a format with real structure is converted and read natively rather than rendered.

variants.title: Route from the real representation
variants.context: The parser route must match the document's actual representation and the downstream output contract. Reusing a trustworthy native text layer is cheaper and more accurate than recognition, and forcing the image path adds latency and recognition error wherever a usable text layer already exists.
variants.prompt: An intake contract labels a batch as scanned, but page probes find a trustworthy native text layer on most pages. What should the router do?
options: Run both routes on every page and keep whichever output is longer.
Honor the intake label and force the image path across the whole batch.
Route on the inspected representation and reuse the trustworthy text layer.
optionFeedback: Longer output is not better output, and running both routes doubles the cost of every page.
A label is a claim about the batch, and forcing recognition over good text adds latency and recognition error.
The inspected representation is the evidence, so pages with a usable layer reuse it and only the rest are recognized.
variants.hint: Ask which signal is evidence and which is only a claim.
variants.explanation: The route follows the document's actual representation, which is why page-level text-layer detection exists instead of a single per-file label.

variants.title: Route from the real representation
variants.context: The parser route must match the document's actual representation and the downstream output contract. Reusing a trustworthy native text layer is cheaper and more accurate than recognition, and forcing the image path adds latency and recognition error wherever a usable text layer already exists.
variants.prompt: To make service times predictable, an operator wants to force the image path for all PDFs so every page costs the same. What is the better plan?
options: Keep automatic routing but switch table analysis off so the slowest stage disappears.
Force the image path, since one predictable cost per page simplifies capacity planning.
Route by representation and benchmark native, scanned, and mixed populations separately.
optionFeedback: Turning off table analysis is only acceptable when losing row and cell relationships is acceptable to the consumer.
Predictability bought by recognizing pages that already have text raises both latency and error for the whole fleet.
Separate benchmarks per population give the p95 and p99 numbers that capacity actually needs without degrading quality.
variants.hint: Ask whether the goal is a stable number or a stable service.
variants.explanation: A benchmark matrix over native, scanned, mixed, table-heavy, and malformed populations replaces a single average without paying recognition cost everywhere.
